response.executiveSummary: NorthBank Payments lets customers initiate card payments from mobile and web banking: requests pass through a gateway to a payments service, are screened for fraud, recorded in a single SQL database, and then queued for a worker that settles them with Visa/Mastercard. The core transaction path is reasonably well authenticated at the edge, but almost every component behind the gateway runs as one instance, and the payments database has no backup, no second zone and no audit logging — so a single storage failure could permanently destroy the record of money movements. The fraud check is also a single unencrypted, unauthenticated internal call, meaning the control that stops fraudulent payments can be bypassed or silently knocked offline. Fixing three things — backups and redundancy for the payments database, redundancy and authentication for the fraud service, and idempotency plus timeouts on the settlement path to the card network — would move this from a system where a bad day means unrecoverable financial loss to one where a bad day means a brief slowdown.
response.businessImpact: The most likely bad day is the payments database failing or being corrupted: every payment stops instantly, customers see errors in the banking app, and because the model shows no backup, no replica and no second region, the record of in-flight and recently settled payments cannot be restored — recovery becomes a manual reconciliation against card network statements lasting days, with regulatory reporting consequences. A second, more frequent bad day is the card network slowing down: with no timeout or circuit breaker, the single settlement worker blocks, the settlement queue backs up, and payments appear to succeed for customers but never actually settle until someone notices.

topRisks.title: The payments database is a single point of total, unrecoverable loss
topRisks.why: One database instance, in one zone, in one region, with no backups holds the authoritative record of customer money movements; losing it halts all payments and destroys the ledger with no restore path.

topRisks.title: Settlement to the card network can hang or double-settle with no protection
topRisks.why: A single settlement worker calls Visa/Mastercard with no timeout, no circuit breaker and no retry policy; a slow card network stalls all settlement silently, while any retry added later without idempotency keys risks double-charging customers.

topRisks.title: The fraud control is a single unauthenticated, unencrypted dependency
topRisks.why: Fraud screening runs on one instance reached over plain HTTP with no authentication, so it can fail and block payments, or be impersonated inside the network to wave fraudulent transactions through.

topRisks.title: The public entry point has no rate limiting, autoscaling or input validation
topRisks.why: An unthrottled public gateway in front of a payments system invites credential stuffing, card testing and volumetric abuse that the two fixed gateway instances cannot absorb, taking the banking app offline for all customers.

topRisks.title: No timeouts or health checks anywhere means failures cascade instead of degrading
topRisks.why: Every synchronous hop — gateway to API, API to database, API to Key Vault — lacks a timeout, and no service exposes a health check, so one slow component exhausts threads upstream and load balancers keep sending traffic to dead instances.

additionalFindings.title: Payment settlement is not idempotent across queue redelivery
additionalFindings.description: Payments API publishes to the Settlement Queue (f5) and the Settlement Worker consumes (f6) and calls the Card Network (f7). Service Bus delivers at least once, and the model shows no idempotency key, deduplication window or transaction identifier on the settlement path. A worker crash after calling the card network but before acknowledging the message will replay the same payment.
additionalFindings.rationale: Duplicate settlement means customers are charged twice for one payment. In a regulated bank this triggers refunds, complaint handling and potential regulatory reporting, and the absence of audit logging on Payments DB makes proving what happened difficult.
additionalFindings.mitigation: Generate a payment idempotency key in Payments API, carry it on the queue message, pass it as the card network idempotency header, and have Settlement Worker check-and-record the key in Payments DB inside the same transaction as the settlement result. Enable Service Bus duplicate detection as a second layer.

additionalFindings.title: Dual write between the payments database and the settlement queue with no outbox
additionalFindings.description: Payments API writes to Payments DB (f4) and separately publishes to the Settlement Queue (f5). The model shows no transactional outbox or saga coordinating the two. If the publish fails after the database commit, a payment is recorded but never settled; if the database write fails after the publish, money moves with no local record.
additionalFindings.rationale: Silent divergence between the ledger and what was actually settled with the card network produces reconciliation breaks that are only discovered at end-of-day, and the missing audit log on Payments DB makes root-causing them slow.
additionalFindings.mitigation: Write the settlement intent to an outbox table in Payments DB in the same transaction as the payment record, and have a relay publish from the outbox to the Settlement Queue. Add a daily automated reconciliation between Payments DB and card network statements.

additionalFindings.title: No dead-letter handling or poison-message strategy on the settlement path
additionalFindings.description: The Settlement Queue feeds a single Settlement Worker (f6) with no modelled dead-letter queue, alerting or replay process. A malformed or repeatedly failing settlement message will either block the subscription or be dropped with no operator visibility, since Settlement Worker also has no health check and no modelled telemetry flow to Monitoring.
additionalFindings.rationale: Failed settlements represent real customer money that never reaches the card network. Without dead-letter visibility these are discovered by customer complaint rather than by monitoring.
additionalFindings.mitigation: Configure a dead-letter queue with max-delivery-count, alert on dead-letter depth and queue age in App Insights, and build a documented replay tool. Add a telemetry flow from Settlement Worker to Monitoring.

additionalFindings.title: Fraud service bypass and spoofing on an unauthenticated internal hop
additionalFindings.description: Flow f3 from Payments API to Fraud Service is plain HTTP with auth 'none' inside the Private Network. Any workload that gains a foothold in that network can impersonate the Fraud Service and return 'approved' for every transaction, or impersonate the Payments API to harvest the transaction stream.
additionalFindings.rationale: The fraud service is the primary anti-fraud control for a payments platform. A control that can be spoofed from inside a flat network provides no real assurance, and the plaintext channel exposes full card transaction detail to anyone able to observe network traffic.
additionalFindings.mitigation: Move f3 to HTTPS with mutual TLS or managed-identity-backed tokens, and treat the fraud service as a separate trust zone with network policy restricting callers to Payments API only.

additionalFindings.title: Fail-open versus fail-closed behaviour of fraud screening is undefined
additionalFindings.description: Fraud Service runs on one replica with no health check and is called synchronously with no timeout or retry (f3). The model does not state what Payments API does when the fraud check is unavailable — approve anyway, or reject all payments.
additionalFindings.rationale: Fail-open turns a routine single-instance outage into a window of unscreened fraudulent payments; fail-closed turns it into a total payment outage. Either way the behaviour should be a deliberate, documented decision rather than an accident of exception handling.
additionalFindings.mitigation: Define and test the degraded-mode policy explicitly (for example, approve below a value threshold and queue for retrospective review above it), add a short timeout and circuit breaker on f3, and run at least two fraud service replicas.

additionalFindings.title: Cardholder and payment data flowing into telemetry is uncontrolled
additionalFindings.description: Payments API sends async telemetry to App Insights (f10) with no stated redaction or sampling policy, and Payments DB has no audit logging and unconfirmed encryption at rest. Payment request payloads typically contain PAN fragments, names and amounts; without explicit scrubbing these end up in a telemetry store with a different access model from the payments database.
additionalFindings.rationale: Cardholder data in logs expands PCI DSS scope to the monitoring platform and its operators, and log stores are commonly accessible to a much wider engineering audience than the payments database.
additionalFindings.mitigation: Add a telemetry redaction filter in Payments API that strips PANs, CVVs and personal identifiers before export, document the retention period for App Insights, and restrict telemetry access to a named group.

additionalFindings.title: Key Vault is a hard synchronous dependency on the payment path with no caching
additionalFindings.description: Payments API calls Key Vault on flow f9 synchronously with no timeout, no retry and no modelled local caching. Key Vault enforces request throttling, so a traffic spike through the unthrottled API Gateway can cause secret retrieval to be throttled and fail the whole payment path.
additionalFindings.rationale: A secrets lookup failure becomes a total payment outage even though the underlying secrets have not changed. This is a common and avoidable cause of self-inflicted downtime.
additionalFindings.mitigation: Cache secrets and certificates in memory with a refresh interval, add a short timeout and bounded retry with jitter on f9, and fall back to the cached value when the vault is unreachable.

additionalFindings.title: Deployment coupling and schema risk from the shared payments database
additionalFindings.description: Both Payments API (f4) and Settlement Worker (f8) write directly to Payments DB. Any schema change must be coordinated across two independently deployed services, and neither connection is modelled with a timeout or retry policy.
additionalFindings.rationale: Shared-schema coupling turns routine releases into coordinated change windows and raises the chance of a deployment-induced outage on the payment path; it also means a runaway query in one service exhausts connections for the other.
additionalFindings.mitigation: Adopt expand-and-contract schema migrations, give each service its own database login with least-privilege table grants and separate connection pools, and set command timeouts on both f4 and f8.

quickWins: Enable automated point-in-time backups and transparent data encryption on Payments DB today, and test a restore.
Set explicit connection and command timeouts on every synchronous call (gateway to API, API to database, API to Key Vault, worker to card network and database).
Turn on rate limiting and quota policies in Azure APIM for all public payment endpoints.
Switch the Payments API to Fraud Service call to HTTPS with mutual TLS and raise the fraud service to two replicas.
Configure a dead-letter queue with alerting on the Settlement Queue and add health check endpoints to all four services.
